## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Predicting community assembly and ecosystem function from measurable traits remains a central challenge in ecology, particularly when organisms face multiple co-occurring environmental stressors whose combined effects are difficult to anticipate. Here we show that a single, cheaply measurable response trait, growth rate measured under matched stressor conditions, is sufficient to predict community composition and biomass yield under factorial stressor combinations. We tested this using synthetic bacterial microcosms exposed to all combinations of temperature, pH and salinity stress, a model system offering full factorial control over stressor regimes. Temperature drove reductions in diversity while salinity drove compositional divergence. A Bayesian growth-rate-to-composition model predicted relative abundances across stress regimes (weighted R² = 0.44); propagating compositional uncertainty into an abundance-weighted mean growth (AWM) metric then predicted endpoint community biomass yield with high accuracy (optical density at 600 nm, OD$_{600}$; R² = 0.88), matching an oracle baseline that used observed rather than predicted compositions. Blocked cross-validation on held-out community identities confirmed that predictions generalise to unseen communities of characterised taxa, and leave-one-stress-out validation showed that composition prediction, though not absolute yield, extends to entirely unmeasured stress regimes. These results demonstrate that when abiotic filtering dominates assembly, a single response trait can bridge the gap from individual physiology to emergent community structure and ecosystem function, and they generate testable predictions for when this trait-based approach should fail in more complex settings.

\newpage

## Introduction

A central goal of community ecology is to predict species composition and ecosystem-level properties from measurable functional traits [@McGill2006; @Violle2007; @Enquist2015; @Kraft2015]. Trait-based approaches have transformed understanding of plant community dynamics [@Enquist2015; @Tilman2004], phytoplankton biogeography [@Follows2007; @Litchman2008], and soil carbon cycling [@Malik2020], establishing the principle that environmental filtering on functional traits can link individual performance to community structure and ecosystem function [@Chesson2000; @McGill2006]. Yet a key test of this principle remains largely unmet: can a single, measurable response trait quantitatively predict multi-species assembly and emergent ecosystem properties when communities face multiple, co-occurring environmental stressors? This challenge is acute because organisms across ecosystems are increasingly exposed to concurrent stressors, including warming, acidification and salinisation [@Kefford2023; @Ct2016; @Schfer2018], whose combined effects often deviate from additive expectations [@Ct2016; @Burgess2021]. Microbial communities, which underpin primary production, decomposition and nutrient cycling across soils, freshwaters and engineered systems [@Cydzik-Kwiatkowska2016; @Newton2011; @Schimel2012; @Cavicchioli2019; @Falkowski2008], offer an especially tractable arena in which to test trait-based prediction under multiple stressors, because of their short generation times, amenability to factorial experimentation, and the growing body of trait-based theory developed for microbial systems [@Litchman2008; @Krause2014; @Malik2020].

One reason trait-based prediction of community assembly remains difficult under multiple stressors is that stressor interactions depend strongly on where organisms sit along non-linear environmental performance curves [@Carmichael2025]. Small changes in stressor intensity can move populations across different regions of their performance curves, switching interactions from antagonistic to synergistic [@Jackson2016]. This performance-curve perspective helps explain variability across multiple-stressor studies [@Simmons2021], but it does not, by itself, provide a quantitative route to forecasting community assembly: which taxa will increase or decline under a given stressor combination, whether stressors drive deterministic environmental filtering versus more contingent dynamics (e.g. priority effects; @Svoboda2018), and how those compositional changes propagate to emergent ecosystem properties such as biomass yield. These two observations suggest a two-step route to prediction: characterise the full nonlinear reaction norms of a set of taxa once, for each stressor singly and in combination, as previously done for the twelve taxa used here [@Carmichael2025], and then test whether growth at the stressor levels a community actually experiences is sufficient to predict its composition and function. The present study delivers that second step.

A tractable route to such forecasts is to use a measurable response trait that integrates stress effects on organismal performance [@Violle2007; @McGill2006; @Krause2014]. If taxa differ in their stress sensitivities, then environmental filtering should systematically reshape community composition as stressors intensify [@Kraft2015]. Intrinsic population growth rate (*r* or $\mu_{\max}$) is a natural candidate response trait: it captures the net effect of stress on physiology and directly translates into biomass accrual during shared growth phases. More broadly, trait-based theory emphasises that trade-offs among growth, stress tolerance and resource acquisition structure communities and drive predictable shifts in composition and function along environmental gradients [@Tilman2004; @Litchman2008], while coexistence depends on stabilising and equalising mechanisms that determine how fitness differences translate into realised abundance [@Chesson2000]. In microbial systems, growth rate is especially amenable to measurement and manipulation, and many community-level outcomes reflect shifts in dominance among fast- and slow-growing lineages [@Newton2011; @Cavicchioli2019; @Krause2014; @Malik2020]. Recent work on synthetic communities has demonstrated that simple assembly rules and beyond-pairwise interactions can enable bottom-up prediction of community structure from component-level measurements [@Friedman2017; @Goldford2018; @Meroz2021; @Ishizawa2024], and that community growth dynamics can be predicted from monoculture growth-curve data [@Ram2019]. The key unresolved question is whether a single stress-specific trait, growth rate, can quantitatively predict multi-taxon assembly under factorial stressor combinations, and whether that signal scales to ecosystem-level biomass yield.

In natural systems, environmental drivers covary, stressors fluctuate, and composition feeds back on local conditions, making it difficult to disentangle the independent and interactive effects of stressors from confounding variation [@Philippot2021; @Choudoir2022; @Justice2017; @Pirotta2022]. Synthetic microbial communities, by which we mean defined communities assembled from known, culturable isolates rather than consortia engineered for a specific task, offer a model-system approach analogous to the use of *Drosophila* or *Arabidopsis* in other fields: they retain key features of real communities (multi-taxon assembly, environmental filtering, emergent biomass production) while allowing stressors, starting composition and environmental history to be manipulated factorially [@Pascual-Garca2025; @Connors2023; @Dolinek2016; @Grokopf2014; @Bengtsson-Palme2020]. This controlled reduction in covariation establishes causal links between stress-specific growth performance, community reassembly and emergent ecosystem properties under conditions where the mapping from individual traits to community outcomes can be tested quantitatively [@Pascual-Garca2025; @Connors2023]. Such empirical benchmarks identify when simple trait-based predictions succeed, generate falsifiable hypotheses for when they should fail (e.g. under strong facilitation, spatial structure or fluctuating environments), and guide translation to more complex natural settings [@Grimm2012; @Liang2022].

Here we use synthetic bacterial microcosms as a model system to test whether a single measurable trait, taxon-level, stress-specific growth rate, can forecast community structure and biomass production across factorial combinations of temperature, pH and salinity. We used a fully factorial 2 × 2 × 2 design (20 vs 38 °C; pH 7.2 vs 5.5; 0 vs 20 g NaCl L$^{-1}$), including all single and combined stressor treatments. These levels were placed on the published performance curves by an explicit protocol, one near-optimal control level and one post-optimum stress level per stressor, in the region where taxon rankings reshuffle across regimes, which is the demanding case for trait-based prediction. Taxon-level growth rates for each stress regime were obtained from previously published monoculture performance curves for these taxa [@Carmichael2025], subset to the experimental stressor levels; we then assembled communities under matched regimes and quantified compositional change and endpoint biomass yield, measured at 48 h, after communities had undergone approximately 5–10 generations of growth and resource-limited competition, a generational depth comparable to that of multi-year grassland experiments [@Tilman2001; @Weisser2017] that provide foundational evidence linking community structure to ecosystem properties, ensuring that communities experienced a full cycle of exponential growth, resource depletion, and competitive exclusion. We also manipulated initial richness to test whether trait-based predictions were robust to starting diversity. Specifically, we ask: **(1)** Do single and combined stressors predictably reshape community diversity and composition? **(2)** Do monoculture growth rates quantitatively predict relative abundance in mixed communities? **(3)** Does integrating trait-based composition predictions with monoculture growth rates forecast community biomass yield across stressor regimes?

## Materials and Methods

### Bacterial taxa

We used twelve heterotrophic bacterial isolates originating from Icelandic geothermal pools and experimental mesocosms in Dorset, England [@Garca2018; @Schaum2017]. These source systems vary in pH, salinity, and temperature; accordingly, the isolates are expected to be adapted to different physicochemical conditions and exhibit diverse tolerance profiles [@Garca2018; @Schaum2017]. Taxa were identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (GenBank accession numbers PX560147--PX560158; **Table S1**). Strains were stored in 20% glycerol stocks at −70 °C and revived by aseptically scraping cells from the frozen glycerol stocks directly into growth medium.

### Multi-stressor response trait

We measured population growth rates for each taxon across all stressor combinations in monoculture to quantify taxon-level stress-responses. Stressor regimes were chosen following a previously published framework [@Carmichael2025], using an environmental performance-curve rationale that defines "stress" relative to each taxon's unimodal growth--environment relationship. We first characterised performance curves for each stressor and identified post-optimum declines. We then selected one near-optimal "control" level and one post-optimum "stress" level for each stressor: temperature (20 vs 38 °C), pH (7.2 vs 5.5), and salinity (0 vs 20 g NaCl L$^{-1}$). Monoculture growth-rate estimates for the eight factorial stressor regimes (2 × 2 × 2; **Table S2**) were then obtained by subsetting these performance-curve datasets to the selected levels, yielding taxon-specific growth rates matched to the stressor regimes used in the community assays (Section 2.3). The monoculture growth-rate inputs used here therefore derive from the performance-curve datasets published in @Carmichael2025; the community assembly experiment, the endpoint 16S sequencing of the assembled communities, and the Bayesian framework scaling taxon-level traits to community composition and biomass are all new to this study. This placement ensures "control" conditions (20 °C, pH 7.2, 0 g NaCl L$^{-1}$) lie within the near-optimal range of the performance curves, while "stress" levels (38 °C, pH 5.5, 20 g NaCl L$^{-1}$) represent reductions from the optimum for most taxa. Monocultures of each taxon were grown in R2A medium (Oxoid, UK; CM0906), with NaCl concentrations set according to the experimental treatment and pH adjusted using sterile 1 M HCl or NaOH as required, and incubated at the target temperature until reaching carrying capacity (typically within \~24 h; assays were run to 48 h to ensure plateau under all stress regimes). Monoculture inocula were prepared as described for the community assays (Section 2.3): stock cultures were revived from −70 °C freezer stocks, pre-cultured in LB medium at 20 °C for approximately 72 h in 48-well plates, transferred to R2A medium and acclimated for 24 h under their respective stressor combinations, then diluted to a common starting density of OD$_{600}$ = 0.05 at the start of the experiment.

Optical density at 600 nm (OD$_{600}$) was recorded every 2 h for the first 12 h and then every \~4 h until OD reached a stationary-phase plateau, using a Varioskan LUX multimode plate reader (Thermo Scientific) with pathlength correction enabled and medium blanks included. For each taxon × condition, growth rates were estimated from monoculture OD data by fitting a Gompertz model to log~10~ (OD$_{600}$) over time (t, in hours):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_{10}\!\bigl(OD_{600}(t)\bigr) = \log_{10}(n_{0}) \;+\; & \bigl[\log_{10}(n_{\max}) - \log_{10}(n_{0})\bigr] \\
& \times \exp\!\Biggl(-\exp\!\biggl(\frac{r \cdot e}{\log_{10}(n_{\max}) - \log_{10}(n_{0})}\,(\lambda - t) + 1\biggr)\Biggr)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-1}
where ${\log}_{10}(n_{0})$ is the starting density, ${\log}_{10}(n_{\max})$ is the carrying capacity, $r$ is the exponential growth rate (h$^{-1}$), and $\lambda$ is the lag time (hours). Nonlinear least-squares regression was implemented in R using 'nls.multstart' [@Padfield2021], initiating 500 random start sets and retaining the converged Gompertz fit with the lowest AIC across starting values (that is, selecting the best-fitting solution for the same model form, not comparing different growth models). Three biological replicates were assayed per taxon under each environmental condition, and the resulting set of monoculture growth rates was retained and treated as the species' stress-response growth rates.

As a sensitivity check on growth-rate estimation, we additionally re-estimated growth rates for every monoculture time series with a model-free log-linear method, taking the steepest slope of log$_{10}$(OD$_{600}$) over rolling windows of consecutive time points within the exponential phase (window widths of 4--8 points), and compared these estimates with the Gompertz estimates used in the pipeline (**Table S23**; **Fig. S9**). To compare the predictive value of alternative monoculture growth parameters, we also refitted the full composition-to-biomass pipeline (Section 2.6) substituting, in place of growth rate, the lag time ($\lambda$) or carrying capacity ($\log_{10} n_{\max}$) obtained from Gompertz fits to the same time series, standardised within stress regimes in the same way (**Table S22**).

### Multi-stressor microbial microcosm experiment

We used synthetic bacterial microcosms to run a fully factorial stressor experiment under controlled and repeatable conditions. Temperature, pH, and salinity were set to predefined levels and applied in combination, while medium composition, incubation duration, and initial inoculation density were standardised across treatments.

We manipulated both single and multiple stressor combinations and the starting taxonomic diversity of our microcosms to investigate impacts on compositional structure and community biomass yield. Communities were assembled at three richness levels: two, four, and eight taxa. For richness two and four, we generated six distinct community compositions per richness; for richness eight, we generated ten compositions. Species compositions were sampled without replacement from the 12-taxon pool using stratified randomisation within each richness level and plate, with edge wells filled with sterile medium to minimise positional effects (**Table S3**). The same set of community identities at each richness level was assayed under each stressor treatment. In total, 22 distinct community compositions (six two-taxon, six four-taxon and ten eight-taxon) were each assembled under all eight stressor regimes, with endpoint OD$_{600}$ and 16S amplicon composition as the response variables. <!-- TODO (Reviewer 2): consider promoting Table S2, plus a design-overview table with replication per treatment x richness, to the main text. -->

Stressor treatments followed a factorial design with high temperature (38 °C), low pH (5.5), and high salinity (20 g NaCl L$^{-1}$), plus their combinations (**Table S2**). Stock cultures were revived from −70 °C freezer stocks, grown in LB medium at 20 °C for approximately 72 h in 48-well plates, then transferred to R2A medium and acclimated for 24 h under the target stressor conditions. pH was adjusted using sterile 1 M HCl or NaOH as required. OD$_{600}$ was measured on the Varioskan LUX using blanks and pathlength correction. Cultures were diluted to a common starting density of OD$_{600}$ = 0.05 (about 1 × 10$^{6}$ cells mL$^{-1}$) in the corresponding medium.

Communities were inoculated into 48-well plates at a total volume of 1.0 mL using a substitutive design (equal total volume, divided among taxa): at richness two, 500 µL per taxon; at richness four, 250 µL per taxon; at richness eight, 125 µL per taxon. Plates were incubated at the designated treatment temperature for 48 h. We chose this duration based on monoculture time-series assays, which showed that all twelve taxa reached stationary phase within approximately 24 h across stress regimes (Figs. S1–S3), and on preliminary community growth curves confirming that mixed communities followed a similar trajectory. The 48 h endpoint therefore captures stationary-phase biomass yield following exponential growth and subsequent resource limitation, encompassing approximately 5–10 generations of population turnover. <!-- TODO (Reviewer 2): state the range of generation numbers across taxa at 20 and 38 C explicitly, computed from the monoculture growth rates (Table S24). --> This generational depth is comparable to that of multi-year grassland experiments [@Tilman2001; @Weisser2017] that provide foundational evidence linking community structure to ecosystem properties; generational turnover provides the relevant ecological timescale for community assembly. Community biomass was measured as OD$_{600}$. Throughout, endpoint OD$_{600}$ is our single measure of total community abundance, and "biomass yield" refers to this endpoint abundance. <!-- TODO (Reviewer 2): decide with co-authors whether to unify OD terminology as "abundance" throughout the text and figures. -->

### DNA extraction and sequencing

Community DNA was extracted using the DNeasy UltraClean Microbial Kit (Qiagen, Netherlands) following the manufacturer's instructions and processed in small batches, including a negative control in every other batch. Extracted samples were stored at −20 °C and processed by Novogene Corporation. DNA was quantified with a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer (dsDNA BR kit, Invitrogen). The V4 to V5 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified with primers 515F (GTGCCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA) and 907R (CCGTCAATTCCTTTGAGTTT)[@Klindworth2013]. PCR reactions (15 µL) contained Phusion High-Fidelity Master Mix (NEB), 0.2 µM of each primer, and approximately 10 ng template DNA. Cycling conditions were: 98 °C for 1 min; 30 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 50 °C for 30 s, 72 °C for 30 s; and 72 °C for 5 min. Amplicons were visualised on 2% agarose gels, purified (Universal DNA Purification Kit, Tiangen), indexed, and sequencing libraries were prepared with the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA PCR-free Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs) with indexes added. Libraries were quality-checked by Qubit, real-time PCR, and Bioanalyzer (Agilent), pooled, and sequenced on Illumina platforms according to effective library concentration and required data yield (Novogene). The expected insert length for 515F to 907R is approximately 392 bp, providing sufficient overlap for paired-end merging.

### Bioinformatic Analysis

Metabarcoding reads were processed with DADA2 [@Callahan2016] in R v4.3.1 [@Team2010]. Residual primers and adaptors were removed with cutadapt [@Martin2011]. Read quality was assessed with FastQC [@SimonAndrews2010] and summarised with MultiQC [@Ewels2016]. Based on quality profiles, reverse reads were truncated at position 241 and reads were filtered with a maximum expected error (maxEE) of 5. Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were inferred with DADA2 (including dereplication, error-model learning, denoising, merging, and chimera removal) to generate the ASV table. Taxonomy was assigned with the naïve Bayesian classifier [@Wang2007] against SILVA v138.1 [@Quast2012]. ASVs with fewer than ten total reads were filtered, and counts were converted to relative abundance with phyloseq [@McMurdie2013]. For downstream phylogenetic analyses, ASVs were aligned with Clustal Omega [@Sievers2011] and a midpoint-rooted tree was constructed. In this defined 12-isolate system, we additionally mapped ASV sequences to isolate 16S reference sequences (PX560147--PX560158) using BLASTn to confirm that dominant ASVs corresponded to the inoculated taxa (**Table S4**). We used the open ASV workflow with SILVA taxonomy, rather than closed-reference mapping to the isolate sequences alone, so that contaminants or unexpected sequence variants would be detected rather than forced onto the inoculated taxa. Relative abundances were not corrected for 16S rRNA gene copy-number variation; because copy number is a stable property of each taxon, this detection bias is consistent across treatments, and systematic per-taxon over- or under-representation is absorbed by the taxon-specific bias term $\delta_{j}$ of the composition model (Eq. 2).

### Data Analysis

All R analysis scripts are available at (https://github.com/GabYvonDurocher/scaling-multiple-stressors).

#### Community diversity and composition analysis

All analyses were performed in R v4.3.1. Endpoint community composition was measured by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (see above), so all diversity and evenness metrics below were computed from ASV relative abundances. ASV counts were converted to relative abundances and ASVs with mean relative abundance $\leq$ 0.5% were removed. Community composition was quantified using Bray--Curtis dissimilarities [@Bray1957]. Differences among stress treatments (Control; pH, Salinity, Temperature; pH×Salinity, pH×Temperature, Salinity×Temperature; pH×Salinity×Temperature) were visualised with distance-based redundancy analysis (db-RDA; 'vegan::capscale') and tested with PERMANOVA ('vegan::adonis2', 9,999 permutations) [@Legendre1999; @Anderson2001; @Oksanen2015]. To check the key PERMANOVA assumption of equal multivariate dispersion among groups, we used 'vegan::betadisper' to compute each sample's distance to its treatment centroid (i.e., the within-group spread in ordination space) and compared these mean distances among treatments; significance was evaluated with permutation tests via 'permutest' on the betadisper model. Pairwise treatment contrasts were obtained with pairwiseAdonis which runs PERMANOVA for every treatment pair on the same distance matrix; the resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini--Hochberg false discovery rate procedure, and effect sizes (R² from each pairwise PERMANOVA) were displayed as a heat map [@MartinezArbizu2020]. Alpha diversity was quantified as Shannon's H′ ('vegan::diversity'). Treatment differences were assessed by permutation ANOVA with Tukey-style post hoc contrasts computed from estimated marginal means ('emmeans') and significance bars relative to the Control [@Lenth2023] . Stress-specific indicator taxa were identified using one-vs-rest indicator species analysis with 'indicspecies::multipatt' and the IndVal.g index, a group-equalised indicator value that combines specificity (how restricted a taxon is to the target group) and fidelity (how consistently it occurs within that group) into a 0–1 score, maximised when a taxon occurs in all samples of, and only in, the focal treatment. Multiple testing was controlled by Benjamini--Hochberg adjustment and significant indicators were reported [@Dufrne1997; @DeCaceres2010; @Petzoldt2019].

#### Bayesian modelling of community composition and biomass

We used a Bayesian statistical model to ask a simple question: given each taxon's growth rate under a particular stress regime, can we predict what the community will look like and how much biomass it will produce? The model takes monoculture growth rates as input, predicts each taxon's relative abundance in a mixed community, and then translates those predicted compositions into community-level biomass yield, propagating uncertainty at each step.

Community composition was modelled using relative abundances. Relative abundances are proportions: they are always non-negative and they always add up to one. To ensure our predictions obey these rules automatically, we used a multinomial-logistic (softmax) link function. The softmax takes one score per taxon and turns the whole set into proportions that sum to one. This means no matter what values the model assigns to taxa, the resulting predictions are always valid compositions.

Each taxon's score was built from its growth trait and some additional effects. Specifically, for sample *n* and taxon *j*, the score was
$$\eta_{nj} = \kappa_{s_{n},r_{n}}\, g_{nj}^{z} + \delta_{j}$$ {#eq-2}

Here, $g_{nj}^{z}$ is the growth rate of taxon *j* in sample *n*, standardised (z-scored) within the corresponding stress treatment by subtracting the stress-specific mean and dividing by the stress-specific standard deviation. This made growth values comparable across each stress regime and also stabilised model fitting. The coefficient $\kappa_{s_{n},r_{n}}$ is a slope that links growth to abundance and is allowed to vary with stress (pH, salinity, temperature) and richness. The main analysis reports these stress-specific slopes. The final term, $\delta_{j}$, is a taxon-specific bias. This bias captures systematic deviations that cannot be explained by growth alone, for example, taxa that are consistently under- or over-represented compared to their growth. Because the softmax is unchanged if the same constant is added to all taxa, we fixed one bias to zero so that the others are interpretable relative to it.

Once the scores were defined, the expected composition for sample *n* was given by
$$p_{n} = \text{softmax}\left( \eta_{n} \right),$$ {#eq-3}

which guarantees $\sum_{j = 1}^{J_{n}}p_{nj} = 1$ for any community size (2, 4, or 8).

Observed data were proportions (relative abundances), so we used a Dirichlet distribution as the likelihood. The Dirichlet is the natural probability distribution for compositional vectors: it only produces non-negative values and it forces the components to sum to one. We wrote this as
$$p_{n}^{\text{obs}} \sim \text{Dirichlet}\left( \phi_{s_{n}}\, p_{n} \right)$$ {#eq-4}

Where $\phi_{s} > 0$ is a stress-specific concentration parameter. This parameter controls how tightly the observed compositions cluster around the predicted composition. A large $\phi_{s}$ means low variability (observations hug the prediction), while a small $\phi_{s}$ allows more scatter. To avoid numerical problems from exact zeros in observed data, we added a vanishingly small jitter (machine precision) to zero entries and renormalised to sum to one. This stabilises computation but has no practical effect on results.

Before fitting, the data were prepared to reflect the experimental design. Each community had a predefined membership of two, four, or eight taxa. If a taxon was inoculated into the starting community but not detected at the end of the experiment, we inserted a zero and renormalised so the community still summed to one. This ensured that absence was treated as true absence, not as missing data. Stress treatments and richness levels were harmonised across data tables, and growth rates were merged in. For the composition model we used the stress-standardised values $g^{z}$, but we retained the raw growth rates $g^{raw}$(in physical units) for the biomass mapping step described below**.** For each taxon under each stress, replicate growth rates were averaged, and only samples with complete growth values for all inoculated community members were retained.

To stabilise estimation and avoid overfitting, we used hierarchical priors. The slopes $\kappa_{s,r}$ had a normal prior centred at zero with a shared variance term, shrinking them toward zero unless supported by the data. The biases $\delta_{j}$ had a similar shrinkage prior with the identifiability constraint already mentioned. The log of the concentration parameter $\phi_{s}$ was given a normal prior, which ensures positivity on the original scale. These priors allow information sharing across stresses and taxa while preventing extreme estimates in poorly informed cases.

Model fitting was done with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) in Stan. We ran four chains and assessed convergence by requiring all parameters to have $\widehat{R} \leq 1.01$, adequate effective sample sizes, and no divergent transitions after warm-up. Full details of the HMC implementation, including chain length, warm-up, adapt_delta, tree depth, seed caching, and convergence diagnostics, are provided in Supplementary Methods S1.

Predictive performance was assessed in several ways. Per-sample log-likelihood contributions were recorded and used with Pareto-smoothed leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) to check how well the model predicted held-out data. We examined the Pareto *k* diagnostics to ensure the approximation was reliable. To measure how close predictions were to observations, we compared posterior mean compositions to the observed proportions using root-mean-square error (RMSE) and Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD). These metrics were reported for each stress regime and globally. For global summaries we weighted by observed abundance so that rare taxa did not dominate the evaluation. As a posterior predictive check, for a random subset of samples we generated new compositions from a Dirichlet distribution centred at the predictions and compared them to the observed using JSD.

To carry uncertainty forward into predicting community biomass, we transformed each posterior draw into an abundance-weighted mean growth (AWM) for each community *c* under stress *s*. For draw *d* this was
$$\text{AWM}_{\text{cs}}^{\text{d}} = \sum_{j}^{}p_{csj}^{d}\, g_{csj}^{\text{raw}}$$ {#eq-5}

Where $p_{csj}^{d}$ is the posterior abundance of taxon *j* and $g_{csj}^{raw}$ is its raw growth rate. This provides a distribution of community-level growth rates that reflect both uncertainty in composition and variability in single-taxon growth rates.

We then related biomass, measured as OD$_{600}$, to AWM with a linear model that included stress and richness effects:

$$\text{OD}_{\text{cs}} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1,s}\,{\bar{AWM}}_{cs} + \beta_{s} + \beta_{r} + \varepsilon,\quad\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\left( 0,\sigma^{2} \right)$$ {#eq-6}

Here, $\beta_{0}$ is the intercept; $\beta_{1,s}$ is the slope linking AWM to ${OD}_{600}$, which was allowed to vary among stress regimes in the model as fitted (18 parameters in total); $\beta_{s}$ denotes stress effects (contrasts relative to a reference level); $\beta_{r}$ denotes richness effects; and $\varepsilon$ is residual error. We also report the additive specification with a single common slope $\beta_{1}$ (11 parameters), under which the conclusions are unchanged, and a fixed-effects-only null model containing the stress and richness terms but no AWM term (10 parameters), which quantifies the marginal contribution of the trait term (**Table S19**). Because endpoint ${OD}_{600}$ in batch culture reflects biomass yield after an initial exponential phase and subsequent stationary phase, we do not assume that community-mean growth mechanically determines yield; instead, Eq. 6 estimates an empirical mapping from AWM to ${OD}_{600}$ while allowing stress and richness to shift expected biomass. Rather than fit Eq. 6 once to a single point estimate of AWM, we refit the OD--AWM regression across a subsample of posterior draws (400 draws): for each draw $d$, we computed $AWM^{d}$, refit Eq. 6, and pooled predictions across draws. This "multiple-imputation" approach propagates uncertainty from composition (and hence AWM) into the reported ${OD}_{600}$ prediction intervals.

To quantify strict out-of-sample performance of the full analysis pipeline (composition model → AWM → OD prediction), we performed blocked five-fold cross-validation in which entire community identities (Com_Id) were held out from model fitting. In each fold, the Dirichlet--softmax model was fit to the training communities only, posterior compositions were predicted for the held-out communities, and composition accuracy on the test set was summarised using RMSE and Jensen--Shannon divergence. We then propagated the predicted compositions to abundance-weighted mean growth (AWM) and fit the OD regression on the training set only; the fitted regression was used to predict OD for the held-out communities, and OD performance was summarised by test-set RMSE and R². Within each fold, stress-specific standardisation parameters (mean and SD) used to compute $g^{z}$ were estimated from the training data only and then applied to the held-out communities, to avoid information leakage across folds.

To test generalisation across environments rather than across communities, we additionally performed leave-one-stress-out (LOSO) cross-validation: each of the eight stress regimes was held out in turn, the composition model was fitted to the remaining seven regimes only, and compositions were predicted for the held-out regime. Because the held-out regime contributes no data to the fit, its stress-specific slope $\kappa_{s}$ and concentration $\phi_{s}$ are informed only by the hierarchical priors and shrink to the across-stress means, which is the appropriate prediction for an unseen environment. The OD regression in this analysis was fitted on the training regimes without stress terms (OD ~ AWM + richness), because stress-specific intercepts and slopes cannot be estimated for a regime absent from training; LOSO is therefore a strictly harder test than the blocked community-identity CV. Within-stress standardisation of growth rates uses only monoculture data, an exogenous input measured independently of the communities, so no community-level information leaks from the held-out regime.

Performance was placed in context with three baselines. An 'oracle' benchmark used the observed compositions to compute AWM, which represents the best possible case if community composition were known exactly. An 'equal-abundance' baseline gave each planned member the same share, a naïve null model. A 'random' baseline drew compositions from a symmetric Dirichlet, representing stochastic assembly without growth information. Comparing against these baselines showed how much was gained by linking monoculture growth rates to community composition and carrying uncertainty forward into biomass predictions.

## Results

### Alpha diversity and community composition across stressor treatments.

We assessed the impacts of temperature, pH, and salinity (and their combinations) on the compositional structure of the eight-taxon communities under the factorial design (temperature 20 vs 38 °C, pH 7.2 vs 5.5, salinity 0 vs 20 g NaCl L$^{-1}$; **Table S2**). Shannon diversity (H′) was similar in the control, pH, and salinity treatments, but declined across all temperature-involving regimes (one-way ANOVA: F₍~7,72~₎ = 26.84, P < 10$^{-17}$; @fig-1). The lowest H′ occurred under the pH × temperature regime, with intermediate values under salinity × temperature and the three-stressor regime. Tukey post hoc contrasts confirmed that each temperature-involving treatment had lower H′ than the control, whereas control vs pH and control vs salinity were not significant after adjustment (full pairwise tests, effect sizes, and 95% CIs in **Table S5**).

Distance-based redundancy analysis (db-RDA) revealed a dominant gradient along RDA1 that explained 80.9% of the constrained variance, separating temperature-involving communities toward positive RDA1 from salinity-influenced communities toward negative RDA1, with control and pH clustering intermediately and showing broad overlap (@fig-1). Community composition differed among treatments (PERMANOVA R² = 0.43, P = 0.001). The strongest pairwise separation was salinity vs temperature (R² = 0.55, adjusted P = 0.028), while comparisons among temperature-involving regimes were not significant after correction (adjusted P > 0.28), indicating partial compositional overlap within the temperature cluster (@fig-1). The full pairwise PERMANOVA matrix is provided in **Table S6**.

Indicator-taxon analysis identified distinct associations with stress regimes (@fig-1). *Janthinobacterium* sp. characterised the control (IndVal.g = 0.89), *Aeromonas* sp. the salinity treatment (0.89), and *Microbacterium* sp. the elevated-temperature treatments (0.81). *Pseudomonas fluorescens* was most strongly identified as an indicator under salinity × temperature combinations, with a weaker association under pH × temperature, and no indication for temperature alone. Complete indicator lists with IndVal.g scores are provided in **Table S7**.

Boxes show medians and interquartile ranges, whiskers denote 1.5 $\times$ IQR, and points represent individual communities (*n* = 30 per treatment). ### Taxon-level stress response growth rates

We measured population growth rates for each taxon across all stressor combinations in monoculture to quantify a taxon-level stress-response trait (growth rate) and test whether stressor-driven shifts in community structure could be explained by this trait. These growth rates were measured under the same eight factorial stress regimes used in the community experiment (**Table S2**), and replicate values were then standardised within each stress regime for comparison across taxa. To compare taxa across stress treatments, we standardised growth rates to within-treatment z-scores, expressed as the number of standard deviations from the treatment mean. Positive scores indicate above-average performance for that stress, and negative scores indicate below-average. This places growth rates on a common scale, enabling direct comparison of relative sensitivities and tolerances across taxa. We visualised replicate distributions alongside taxon means (@fig-2). Rankings were treatment specific: different taxa performed best under different stressors, though some overlap occurred in temperature-involving treatments. For example, temperature tended to favour *Microbacterium* sp., salinity favoured *Aeromonas* sp., and acidic pH elevated *Janthinobacterium* sp. These z-score patterns were broadly consistent with the indicator-species analysis, with high z-score taxa matching positive indicators for the corresponding treatments. See **Table S8** for the z-score summary by stress × taxon and **Table S24** for the raw growth-rate estimates underlying the z-scores.

Across stresses, dispersion was similar (SD $\approx$ 0.89--1.03); the total span was largest for pH $\times$ salinity (range $\approx$ 3.82) and also wide for temperature ($\approx$ 3.52). Taxon rankings were treatment-specific: *Microbacterium* sp. tended to score highest under elevated temperature, *Aeromonas* sp. under salinity, and *Janthinobacterium* sp. under acidic pH, consistent with the indicator-species analysis.](../results/figures/Fig_2_DOTPLOT_z_by_stress_compact.png){#fig-2 fig-pos="htbp"}

### Trait-based prediction of composition and biomass

Having established how stressors reshape diversity and composition, we asked whether taxon-level stress response growth rates could predict community outcomes. We used a two-stage Bayesian framework: first, a softmax composition model (a statistical function that converts continuous scores into proportions summing to one) mapped standardised, stress-specific growth rates to relative abundances; second, predicted compositions were converted to an abundance-weighted mean growth and linked to OD$_{600}$ to predict community biomass. For each assembled community we supplied the model with the set of taxa present, the stress regime, and the taxa's stress-specific growth rates. The model mapped growth rates to relative abundances via a Bayesian softmax, yielding full posterior distributions for composition. In-sample posterior predictive checks showed that this growth-rate-to-composition mapping reproduced observed taxonomic composition endpoints (48 h, @fig-3). To test whether this performance generalises to unseen communities assembled from these characterised taxa, we performed blocked five-fold cross-validation (blocking by community identity, Com Id, **Fig. S6**). Across folds, out-of-sample composition predictions were stable (mean RMSE = 0.131 $\pm$ 0.040 SD; mean JS = 0.089 $\pm$ 0.011 SD) and composition accuracy was broadly similar across stress regimes (**Table S16**; fold-wise CV summaries in **Table S15**; overall CV summary in **Table S18**). Predicted relative abundances explained 44% of the weighted variance in observations (weighted $R^{2} = 0.44$; weighted RMSE = 0.22) (@fig-3).

![**Growth-based predictions of community composition and biomass across stress regimes.** Posterior predictive accuracy for relative taxon abundances across all stress treatments and richness levels (**a**). Points show observed versus posterior mean predictions; horizontal bars indicate 90% credible intervals. Colour denotes stress treatment and shape denotes richness. The dashed line is the 1:1 line. Weighted metrics (wRMSE = 0.22; wR$^2$ = 0.44) summarise global predictive performance. Posterior predictive accuracy for total community biomass (OD$_{600}$ at 48 h) based on abundance-weighted mean growth (AWM) (**b**). RMSE = 0.10, R$^2$ = 0.88. The model conditions on predefined community membership (2, 4, or 8 taxa).](../results/figures/Fig_3.png){#fig-3 fig-pos="htbp"}

To extend from composition to biomass, we combined the predicted relative abundances from the model with the measured monoculture growth rates of each taxon. For each community this yielded an abundance-weighted mean growth rate, essentially the average single-taxon growth ability weighted by how abundant each taxon was predicted to be. This community-level value was then linked directly to measured OD$_{600}$, so that predicted biomass reflected both the mix of taxa and their intrinsic growth. The output was a distribution of biomass predictions for each community that incorporated the uncertainty in composition. Biomass was also recovered accurately: predictions matched observations quantitatively (RMSE = 0.10; $R^{2} = 0.88$) and clustered around the 1:1 line (@fig-3). In the same blocked five-fold cross-validation, OD predictions remained strong out of sample (mean RMSE = 0.117 $\pm$ 0.036 SD; mean R² = 0.783 $\pm$ 0.172 SD across folds, **Fig. S7**), although performance varied among folds (**Table S15,** overall CV summary in **Table S18**). Fold-to-fold differences were attributable to the OD range represented in the held-out data: Fold 5, which had the narrowest OD range and highest minimum biomass (**Table S17**), yielded the lowest R² (0.49), consistent with reduced predictive discrimination when communities cluster in a compressed, high-biomass region of the response space. Performance was consistent across stress regimes and richness classes, with no single treatment dominating the error structure (in-sample per-regime RMSE/R² and LOO in **Tables S9--S10**; composition fits in **Fig. S4**; blocked out-of-sample CV by Com_Id in **Tables S15--S18**). To benchmark predictive skill, we compared our growth-based model against three baselines (**Fig. S5**; **Table S11**): (i) equal-abundance (uniform shares), (ii) random composition (Dirichlet draws), and (iii) an 'oracle' benchmark given the observed compositions, i.e. the best possible case if community composition were known exactly. The growth-based model outperformed both naïve baselines and achieved accuracy comparable to the oracle (ΔRMSE = −0.01 OD$_{600}$; ΔR² = +0.01), confirming that predictive power derives from trait–environment matching rather than from trivial composition assumptions (model-comparison details in **Tables S12–S13**). To isolate the marginal contribution of the trait term itself, we decomposed the biomass model (**Table S19**): the stress and richness effects alone explained half the variance in community biomass (R² = 0.50), adding the AWM term as a single additional parameter raised this to 0.84, and the full model with stress-specific slopes reached 0.88 (partial R² over the null: 0.68 for the additive trait term, 0.76 for the full set of trait terms; joint test of the trait terms in the full model: F(8,153) = 61.9, *P* < 10$^{-43}$; AWM coefficient t = 18.5; **Table S19**). The equal-abundance baseline (R² = 0.77) is itself not a trait-free benchmark, as it retains the monoculture growth rates while discarding the composition weighting; the decomposition therefore forms a ladder: no trait, R² = 0.50; trait without composition information, 0.77; trait with trait-predicted composition, 0.88.

To test generalisation across environments, we held out each stress regime in turn (leave-one-stress-out CV; Methods). Composition prediction for entirely unseen regimes was essentially as accurate as for unseen communities (mean RMSE = 0.136 $\pm$ 0.009 SD; mean JS = 0.093 $\pm$ 0.020 SD across the eight held-out regimes, **Table S20**; compare RMSE = 0.131 $\pm$ 0.040 for the blocked community-identity CV, **Table S18**), indicating that the hierarchical structure of the composition model transfers the growth-to-abundance mapping to unmeasured regimes. Absolute biomass yield, by contrast, did not extrapolate: with no stress terms estimable for a held-out regime, OD predictions degraded sharply (mean RMSE = 0.293 $\pm$ 0.101; within-regime R² was negative for six of eight regimes; **Tables S20--S21**, **Fig. S8**), reflecting regime-specific shifts in the AWM-to-yield mapping that cannot be recovered from the trait alone. Trait-based composition prediction thus generalises across environments, whereas yield prediction requires the focal stress regime to be represented in the calibration data.

Growth rate was also the most informative of the monoculture growth parameters. Substituting lag time or carrying capacity for growth rate in the same pipeline sharply degraded composition prediction (weighted R² = 0.08 and 0.11 respectively, versus 0.44 for growth rate) and biomass prediction (R² = 0.77 and 0.55, versus 0.88; **Table S22**). The conclusions were also robust to how growth rate is estimated: model-free log-linear estimates correlated strongly with the Gompertz estimates (Pearson r = 0.95; Spearman ρ = 0.94 overall, and 0.78--0.97 within regimes; **Table S23**, **Fig. S9**), and rerunning the pipeline with log-linear estimates left biomass prediction unchanged (R² = 0.89) with moderately lower composition accuracy (weighted R² = 0.30; **Table S22**), consistent with the composition model's reliance on within-regime rank differences among taxa.

## Discussion

Our results show that taxon-level growth rates predict how multi-taxon communities assemble across single and combined stressors (20 vs 38 °C; pH 7.2 vs 5.5; 0 vs 20 g NaCl L$^{-1}$), and that these growth-driven shifts in composition scale to forecast community biomass yield. The success of a single-trait model, and its near-equivalence to an oracle using observed compositions, indicates that under strong abiotic filtering, the mapping from monoculture performance to community outcome is both tractable and quantitatively accurate.

This predictive success rested on distinct, stressor-specific filtering mechanisms that reshaped community composition in different ways. Temperature was the dominant driver of alpha diversity: Shannon diversity declined exclusively in temperature-involving treatments, consistent with warming amplifying fitness differences along thermal performance curves, narrowing the realised niche space for thermally sensitive taxa (@fig-1). By contrast, pH and salinity maintained diversity near control levels when applied individually, reshaping composition without reducing evenness. The db-RDA ordination confirmed a dominant temperature–salinity gradient, with temperature-involving communities clustering together while salinity-influenced communities separated in the opposite direction; pH alone overlapped with controls. Temperature and salinity thus acted as largely orthogonal filters, imposing distinct physiological constraints (protein stability and membrane homeostasis under warming; osmotic balance under salinity [@Gregory2021; @Petrosyan2024; @Renne2023; @Terradot2024]), whose net effects are captured by the measured performance trait, growth rate. Indicator-taxon analysis reinforced these patterns: *Janthinobacterium* sp. characterised control communities, *Microbacterium* sp. elevated-temperature treatments, and *Aeromonas* sp. salinity treatments (@fig-1).

Crucially, monoculture assays showed that taxon rankings reversed across stress regimes: taxa that performed best under one stressor were not consistently superior under another (@fig-2). This stress-specific reshuffling is the essential prerequisite for growth-rate-based prediction: if rank order were invariant, composition would be dominated by the same taxa regardless of environment, and stressor interactions would reflect uniform suppression rather than reassembly.

In closed batch microcosms, taxa that divide faster under a given stress regime accrue more biomass during the shared growth phase, and under substitutive inoculation this advantage compounds: small initial differences in growth rate yield large differences in relative abundance by the endpoint. Because community biomass aggregates the contributions of each member, stress-driven dominance shifts towards faster growers tended to increase total yield in our system. We note that this is an empirical association rather than a necessity: resources are finite, endpoint yield is bounded by carrying capacity, and a higher growth rate does not automatically imply a higher carrying capacity, which is why Eq. 6 estimates the mapping from abundance-weighted growth to yield empirically rather than assuming it. Growth rate thus acts as both a response trait that mediates environmental filtering and, via abundance weighting, a predictor of community biomass production. These growth-rate advantages accrued over a substantial generational depth: monoculture assays confirmed that all twelve taxa reached stationary phase within approximately 24 h across stress regimes (Figs. S1–S3), with community growth trajectories following a similar pattern; the 48 h endpoint therefore captures composition shaped by both exponential growth and extended stationary-phase resource limitation, spanning approximately 5–10 generations, comparable to the generational depth of multi-year grassland experiments [@Tilman2001; @Weisser2017] that provide foundational evidence linking community structure to ecosystem properties.

Given these conditions, our models successfully predicted community composition across stressor regimes, demonstrating that stress-matched growth rates measured in isolation capture much of the assembly signal in these simplified communities (@fig-3). The Bayesian softmax framework mapped stress-standardised growth rates to relative abundances, producing probabilistic composition forecasts that quantify uncertainty. Importantly, the model's success does not imply that biotic interactions are absent; rather, it indicates that in well-mixed batch culture with substitutive inoculation, where abiotic filtering dominates over biotic interactions, the component of assembly driven by stress-dependent growth differences is large enough to be predictive.

The extension from composition to biomass prediction shows how community-level properties such as biomass yield can emerge from abundance-weighted growth-rate distributions (@fig-3). By combining posterior compositions with raw monoculture growth rates to compute abundance-weighted mean growth before mapping this to endpoint OD$_{600}$, we operationalised a community-weighted mean trait approach [@Enquist2015] under factorial multi-stressor conditions. The trait-based pipeline outperformed naïve null models, achieving comparable accuracy to an "oracle" that used observed compositions, indicating that predictive power derives from trait--environment matching rather than from trivial composition assumptions. That biomass prediction accuracy (R² = 0.88) substantially exceeds composition accuracy (weighted R² = 0.44) likely reflects the disproportionate contribution of dominant taxa to total OD$_{600}$: because the model predicts the most abundant taxa more accurately than rare ones, errors in the tail of the abundance distribution have limited effect on the aggregate biomass forecast. A related, systematic feature is that the composition model underpredicts the most dominant taxa: the shrinkage inherent in the Dirichlet--softmax formulation pulls extreme predicted abundances towards the community mean, a conservative bias that trades some accuracy for dominant taxa against stability of the overall fit. This near-equivalence to the oracle suggests that, under strong abiotic filtering, knowing each taxon's growth rate under a given stress regime is as informative as knowing the true community composition, a finding with practical implications, since monoculture growth assays are far simpler to conduct than community-level compositional surveys. This economy is compounded by the two-step structure of the approach: reaction norms need be characterised only once, from a modest number of levels per stressor [@Carmichael2025], after which community composition can be predicted at any regime on those curves without further community-level measurement; predicting absolute yield at a new regime additionally requires the regime-specific yield mapping to be calibrated against community data. This dominance-driven accuracy also suggests that the approach is most likely to generalise in systems where a few taxa dominate biomass, a widespread feature of microbial communities, whose abundance distributions are typically highly skewed regardless of environmental context [@Shoemaker2017].

These findings have direct implications for applied microbial ecology. In engineered systems such as wastewater bioreactors, industrial fermentation, and bioremediation, stressor regimes are specified by design and monoculture growth assays for component taxa are routine [@Lindemann2016; @Lawson2019]. A trait-based pipeline that maps growth performance to compositional and yield outcomes could therefore support rational design of microbial consortia and process optimisation. Similarly, in synthetic community design for agriculture and industrial bioprocessing, where defined species pools are assembled under controlled conditions, growth-rate-based forecasting provides a quantitative starting point for predicting community behaviour before scale-up. The quantitative framework established here offers a tractable complement to the broader set of engineering principles emerging for microbiome design [@Lawson2019].

Our growth-rate-to-composition and growth-rate-to-biomass mappings are most likely to hold when (i) abiotic stress is the dominant filter, (ii) communities experience a shared growth phase with broadly common resources, and (iii) interaction outcomes are not strongly shaped by frequency-dependent mechanisms [@RossGillespie2007]. Leave-one-stress-out cross-validation makes one boundary concrete: the growth-to-composition mapping transferred to entirely unmeasured stress regimes with essentially undiminished accuracy, whereas absolute yield did not extrapolate, because stress regimes shift the overall mapping from abundance-weighted growth to yield in ways that must be estimated from community data for the focal regime (**Tables S20--S21**; **Fig. S8**). Several ecological processes can weaken the link between monoculture growth and community dominance: cross-feeding and facilitation, interference competition (for example, toxins), priority effects, spatial structure, and consumer control can all allow slower-growing taxa to persist or dominate despite lower intrinsic growth [@Kerr2002; @Fukami2015; @Connors2026; @Athreya2025; @Mehlferber2024]. Over longer timescales, adaptation may alter growth rankings under stress [@Lenski2017]. In open systems with continual immigration or fluctuating environments, transient dynamics and eco-evolutionary feedbacks could further weaken the trait–composition link [@Hairston2005]. These boundaries motivate follow-on tests in larger species pools and in systems approaching steady state (for example, chemostats) where resource competition and interaction networks can be quantified explicitly [@vandenBerg2022]. Understanding when growth-rate-based predictions break down will require integrating ecological modelling approaches that account for emergent community properties arising from species interactions [@vandenBerg2022].

## Conclusions

Our results support a mechanistic route by which multiple stressors scale from taxon-level growth performance to community-level biomass: stressors reshape growth-rate ranks, altered ranks shift relative abundances through environmental filtering, and abundance-weighted growth distributions predict community biomass yield. This pathway provides an empirically grounded proof of principle, with quantitative, testable benchmarks, for forecasting microbial community responses when abiotic filtering is strong and growth rate can be measured under matched stress regimes. The approach generates clear, testable predictions for when it should fail: as biotic interactions strengthen, spatial structure develops, evolutionary change alters growth-rate rankings, or fluctuating environments favour bet-hedging strategies over maximal growth. Extending this framework to broader species pools, open systems such as chemostats, and longer timescales will determine how far growth-rate-based forecasting can generalise. These tests will reveal when additional traits (survival under stress, resource-use efficiency, interaction-mediated effects) become necessary, and will establish the quantitative boundaries within which single-trait prediction remains a reliable forecasting tool.
